utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Registrar. This is Thursday, January the 29th [as interpreted], 2009. I would like to welcome the witness, to greet the accused, the counsels, and all the members of the OTP, as well as all those assisting us in the courtroom. Yesterday, I told you that in the afternoon, the Chamber would file its decision on the Prosecution's motion to obtain an adequate summary of Slobodan Bozic's statement. This is statement -- the decision could not be recorded. I'm going to read it out to you, at least the operative part. In the light of this in compliance with Articles 64 and 65 ter (G) of the Rules, grants the motion, partially grants the supplementary motion, orders the Stojic Defence to complement the 65 ter summary of Witness Slobodan Bozic, as explained here above, at the latest by January 23rd, 2009; stays its decision on the part of the motion pertaining to the 65 ter summary of Stijepo Buljon [phoen], of the witness Stijepo Buljon and rejects for the remainder the supplementary motion. So, in a word, in a nutshell, the Stojic Defence is asked to complement the summary in the way described in the recitals, but you will see this because this decision will be filed very shortly. So, anyhow, the witness is going to come next week. Let us move on, and I now give the floor to Ms. Alaburic, who has only a few minutes left. I do not know exactly how many, but you have very few minutes left. The Registrar is going to tell me how many minutes you have left. The floor is yours, Ms. Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your indulgence, just one moment. It's not clear from the transcript, and I didn't catch it in the translation, the date by which the Defence for Mr. Stojic is ordered to supplement, in accordance with your oral decision, the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 23rd of January, at the latest. Yes, sorry, I failed to notice that it hadn't been written in the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, good morning to you, and good morning to you, Mr. Marijan and everybody else in the courtroom. According to our records and as far as we have been told by the Registry, I have 26 more minutes to go.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So, Mr. Marijan, we're going to start with some clarifications about what you said in examination-in-chief. The first --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, let's check this, because there was -- the legal officer was a bit puzzled, but let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continued] ... that I'd like to question you about is the transcript of the conversation between President Tudjman and the representatives of Herceg-Bosna, held on the 10th of November, 1993, and it is document P 6581. The Defence of Bruno Stojic, Mr. Marijan, asked you about a portion of that transcript which is to be found on pages, in the Croatian version, 0132-3063 -- I apologise, I gave the wrong page. Let me repeat the correct page. 0132-3073, and in the English version, it is page 1D 570071 -- 570071. Mr. Marijan, you needn't bother to look for the document. You can find it on the screen, and I'm going to talk to you about just one --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, according to the Registrar, you have another six minutes and not twenty-six, unless you have received some time from Mr. Coric's Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, we said yesterday and the day before that General Praljak will cede some of his time to me. General Praljak used 12 minutes, so the 18 minutes that belonged to the Praljak Defence has now been placed at the disposal of the Petkovic Defence, which makes 26 minutes altogether.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So if we can go back to the document, the document is otherwise to be found in the Stojic Defence binder. The Stojic Defence asked you a question about a statement made by President Tudjman, and I'm going to quote your words recorded on transcript page 74 on Tuesday, line 9, to the effect that the minister of the defence will not be in command of the army -- will not command the army. You can look at that on the screen, and you'll see what was said. And your comment was that President Tudjman was aware of the authorities of the minister of defence in Herceg-Bosna and that the statement made was correct. Have I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, good morning, Your Honours. Yes, you did understand me correctly, Madam.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now I'd like you to read out the beginning of that statement made by President Tudjman, word by word.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Army, he will not command the army directly ..."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Very well. Now, tell me, if we were to compare what you say and what you said during the examination-in-chief, it follows that in-chief, you left out the word "directly" and that you didn't comment the statement made by President Tudjman to the effect that he will not command the army directly, and from which it would be logical to conclude that he can command indirectly. Now, tell me, the fact that you left out the word "directly," may we have your comments on that? How do you comment that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, Your Honours, I'm not quite sure -- are you quite sure that I quoted this? Because I was asked to comment, and that's what I did, I commented.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But you didn't comment on the word "directly." In your comment, you left out the word "directly," so I'm asking you now, why did you leave the word "directly" out?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you read out, you said that I said "minister," so it wasn't an actual quotation. You said that I said that the minister would not, but -- so it's not a quotation, it's my comment.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Now I'm asking you why, in your comment, you left out the word "directly."

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know why I left it out. All I can say is, well, command of the army becomes -- is direct, so I don't see why -- what you mean when you say "indirect," "indirectly."

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm just interested in your understanding of certain statements, and whether you leave out a concept or word or not, we're going to be able to weigh out -- or, rather, Their Honours will be able to weigh the worth of your statements. So I'd like to clear this up. This word "directly," you, as an expert witness of the Stojic Defence, do you consider this word "directly" to be relevant or not?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it is just irrelevant here in this context, completely irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right, fine. I'd like to ask you to explain, because I consider it's relevant for the full understanding of your testimony if you were to do so, and it has to do with the following: Your report ends by looking at a meeting of the political leadership of the HZ-HB of the 29th of April, 1993 at which Bruno Stojic asked that a political decision be made about sending military units to Central Bosnia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is right, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And then you ended with the topic of political decision-making about sending military units to Central Bosnia; do I remember that correctly?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said what he called for, what he was asking.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, tell me, do you happen to remember whether at that particular meeting of the 29th of April, 1993, somebody was present from the Main Staff of the HVO, perhaps?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In your report, you claim that Bruno Stojic performed administrative work, administrative business, within the sphere of defence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you explain how come Bruno Stojic, at that meeting of the 29th of April, 1993, asked that a political decision be taken about sending military units to Central Bosnia if his remit was administrative business within the frameworks of defence?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you looked -- well, you insisted upon item 9 yesterday. You insisted upon that a great deal, so -- of the decision on the basis of or the organisational structure of the Defence Department, then you would have seen there that it says that Mr. Stojic, along with his administrative work, that administrative work includes parts related to the armed forces, things related to the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that those administrative affairs include affairs like sending the army to a certain part of Herceg-Bosna in order to engage in combat?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it doesn't, it doesn't include that. That does not come within his remit.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Can you explain how, then, Bruno Stojic, at this meeting, raised that question and asked that a political decision be made in that regard?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the question of a political decision regarding the army ultimately raises the question of organisation and reinforcement to that army, which means that Mr. Stojic could, when it came to material, security, and a series of other affairs, he could weigh up the situation and then could raise a question of that nature.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, with respect to carrying out these administrative affairs, would it be necessary to seek for a political decision or does doing that work, does it imply all this when the army moves to Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if the army moves, advances, then that would imply what you just said.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. But that doesn't call for a political decision, if all this is implied, so do you consider that this request at this political meeting by Bruno Stojic merits additional comment to what you said or not?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right, fine. Now, can we go back to where we left off yesterday, and we left off looking at the diagrams of the military police. And on the subject of the military police, a brief question. Now, military affairs came under the remit of the head of the Defence Department; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's precisely it.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right, fine. Now, tell me, please, if a unit of the military police were to be resubordinated to the commander of some HVO unit in order to engage in combat, then during the time for which it was resubordinated, that military police unit would be responsible to the commander of the HVO; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the unit would be responsible to the commander to whom it was resubordinated.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And that lasts for as long as the resubordination time lasts; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the how it should be.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, Mr. Marijan, tell me this: What we saw about the areas of responsibilities, this line, this chain of responsibility, can we see it in all the reports on the work of the Defence Department and in the programmes or proposals for programmes of work of the Defence Department; would that be true?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you be a bit clearer? I'm not sure I understand you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'll refer you back to your report, where you say that the report on the work of the Main Staff included combat operations and that that is why it was set apart from the Defence Department report and was accessible to the office of the HZ-HB. Is that what you noted in your report?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite certainly, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm sure you did.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't, and I'm sure I didn't, Madam. Would you like to read that portion out?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I will read it out, but I'll do that in due course. But now I'd like to go on with this: The report on the work of the Defence Department included reports on the work of each of the mentioned sectors; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right, so that is what I said. It's not a matter of the fact that the Main Staff reported on combat, but that the fact that the Main Staff is a component part of the Defence Department, and Mr. Stojic didn't have full authority over that. So that's where the problem lies. And you said it a little differently.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: It's not a problem. It's all very simple.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it seems that you think it's very simple.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would you explain what you mean, that it's simple for me, that things are going quite simply for me?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you confused me yesterday at one point.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Just one moment, Mr. Marijan. Before we move on, with Their Honours' permission, because I don't have much time, would you tell us here and now whether during the yesterday's day you discussed yesterday's testimony in this courtroom with anyone, with anybody whatsoever, including telephone conversations?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just talked to my wife about my child.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And your wife, did she discuss this with anyone, the contents of your testimony in this courtroom with anybody else?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: My conversation with my wife was as follows: I said I had a difficult day, and that was it. And, of course, I was interested in how my family was doing. And I can tell you very frankly and sincerely that I didn't discuss it with anyone, but I assume I had the right to think about these things.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Yes, you do have the right to think about things, but we're not going to take my time up with you presenting what you were thinking about. You can do that on some other occasion. And now I'd like to ask you to continue my cross-examination, and I'd like you to clear up the following: In your report, you noted -- well, I owe you an explanation, in actual fact. The portion of your report in which you mention a definition of the Defence Department in the broadest sense, which would include the HVO units and the operative zones, and you weren't able to remember that that was contained in your report, so I'd like to ask you now and remind you now that it is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Alaburic, Ms. Alaburic, I'd like to dwell on the military police issue. I'd like to ask specific questions. Witness, when you were a member of this brigade, the name of which has already been mentioned, did you ever, in combat activities, happen to be present in the field with members of the military police? Did that happen to you or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was in the field, Your Honour, only with the members of the military police of our brigade, which was part of our brigade by establishment. There were no outside units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. So you were with members of the brigade. In those military operations, did the members of the military police of the brigade also fight the enemy? Did they fire-fight back, did they actually participate in the military activity?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I am not aware of any involvement of the military police in any specific case. It was a small unit in Livno that went out into the field, and that smaller unit -- that smaller detail was providing security to the commander or, rather, to the command post to the brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, you did not write that the report on the work of the Main Staff included a report on combat activity and that it was available to the members of the Cabinet of the President of HZ-HB. It was in paragraph 13 of your report, and since you are not aware of the contents of your report, I have to ask you if you really authored this report.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I don't want any further comments, Mr. Marijan. I'd like to deal with item 87 now in your report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, remain calm. One needs to be cool in life, especially here. So please answer the questions and everything will be fine.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I have certain problems at home, and it's taking its toll.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, I think I was very delicate in my approach, and if I could have learned a bit more from Mr. Karnavas, I think it would have helped me.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think Mr. Karnavas was very delicate.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's talk about the point in your report when you talk about the signing of documents. It's P745, paragraph 87, where you present the conclusion based on the enactment and the signing of documents, that all chiefs of units, brigades, and other professional units were not within the jurisdiction of the head of the Defence Department.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This document demonstrates relationships within the Defence Department.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, I'm sorry, I am asking questions here. I'm just asking you, is it true that you noted this in paragraph 87?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's true. It's a general indicator of relationships.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me, have you ever in your life seen a decision of the civilian HVO pursuant to which this decision on signing the documents of the Defence Department was taken?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Look now at document 4D 1279. It's in the third section, third batch of my documents. It's marked "Other Documents." While you are searching, I'll say that it was a decision taken by the HVO at its session of the 14th of October, 1992. It's called "The Decision on the Signing of Documents of the HVO of HZ-HB." In this decision, which was signed by Jadranko Prlic, as you can see, but the decision was taken by the collective body of the HVO, and that's something that Mr. Karnavas asked you about, in Article 2 of this decision it says that the Defence Department got the number 02?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Look at Article 4, where it says that officials of the Defence Department -- can we -- by their respective decisions, the heads of departments shall determine the members to be assigned to the departments on the internal divisions?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: What are these heads of departments?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the security sector that gets a number, parts of the civilian sector which are not divided into administrations, the healthcare sector, and the sector for replenishment and supply, and the main sector.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell me about brigades and operation zones and units. These are not sub-units of the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Would it be logical, then, for the these operation zones, brigades and professional and other units, do not get a signature number, according to this decision?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's logical concerning these units.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to your conclusion from paragraph 87. Based on this decision made by Bruno Stojic, according to which the signature numbers are given only to sub-departments, not brigades and zones, et cetera, you conclude that only the head of the department was under the jurisdiction of the head of the Defence Department. Would you now change this conclusion?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but only the final part, because the upper part is still justified.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: You mean everyone below the chief?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, I made a conclusion that doesn't hold water.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: My colleague tells me that my question was not correctly recorded, so I'll repeat it. Would you now, after seeing this decision of the HVO, this fundamental decision, would you change now your paragraph 87 conclusion, where it says that everything below the chief was not in the jurisdiction of the head of the Defence Department because operation zones, brigades and other units did not get their signature numbers as sub-units of the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: This article was written to show the level up to which the head of department communicates in the Main Staff. Generally speaking, these units were not within his jurisdiction.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: They were not in his jurisdiction or they were not parts of the organisation of the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Along their own line, which we haven't clarified yet, Stojic has the right to communicate with them, and you have shown me a lot of documents to that effect. But he did not --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But, look, even administrative affairs between Bruno Stojic and some brigade, let's say, include communication that would call for the signing of documents?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true, but that's something that the Main Staff decides.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm not going to waste any more time on this. I think things are very clear. Since I do not have much time and I want to go through a number of other topics with you, let us move on. In your report, in several places you claim that the Defence Department was established on the 3rd of July, 1992, by virtue of a Decree on the Armed Forces.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have three minutes remaining. Witness, you spoke quickly, and in the translation that received, that I saw and heard, you said that the Main Staff had the codes. At least I heard that. What did you mean? What did you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In fact, it's the transmission number, a reference number. In this correspondence, in the registers of correspondence, every institution has its own number, its reference number. The Main Staff assigns number to lower units. They start with 00 -- I can't remember exactly, but in the reference number of the document, you can find one part of the number which tells you exactly who created it, regardless of who signed it. So it can contain several numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please give an example.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Specifically, let's take an example that I came across in my unit. The first part of the reference number is the number of the military post box where I was, 1736. Then it goes dash, then the number of the sector to which I belonged. That's political affairs. Let's say it was 08. And if I drafted the document, "08" would be followed by a stroke or a slash, and then would follow my number, "03," and then the general sequential number in our register, including the year the document was created.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So all of the documents should have these references?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, if the records were kept properly, yes. I did not look at the keeping of files and documents elsewhere, but I did look at the HVO, and I found very few units that strictly applied the instruction on the keeping of records.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Was the situation in Herceg-Bosna so well ordered and peaceful that there was no chance for a document to come into or leave an institution without being properly recorded?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The possibility that some things were not recorded always exists.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And you would say that otherwise there was total order, office management was perfect, registers of correspondence were kept perfectly?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you I did not supervise the archiving performed by the HVO. I looked at the archives of the HVO after the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: I'm asking about your general knowledge, as a historian, about the situation in Herceg-Bosna, because some believe that chaos was so complete that it's absolutely out of the question that office management and record-keeping was proper.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It certainly wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I wanted the witness to clarify why he insists repeatedly that the Defence Department was established in July and that the system of defence was established when Bruno Stojic was appointed to his position. I need five minutes for that, Your Honours, and I kindly ask you to grant me these five minutes to deal with this. Let me recall that my colleague Ms. Nozica did get additional time, and so did my learned friend Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to consult with my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have used all of your time, the allotted time, and since the Chamber can grant additional time, we give you an additional five minutes. In five minutes, you can have a lot of things said by the witness. Take example from myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Marijan, in several places you claim that the Defence Department was established on the 3rd of July, 1992, according to the Decree on the Armed Forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think -- let me not look for the specific reference now -- it was established based on the statutory decision on the basics of the organisation on the 3rd of -- taken in May.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So it's true that it was established along with other organs on the 15th of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is mentioned in the decision.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: If I understood correctly, it was only in July with the appointment of the head of the Defence Department that the organisation of the Defence Department really begins, people are being appointed, and certain conclusions are made?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After the 3rd of July, the Defence Department gradually gets organised.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Was the system of the Defence Department already defined in July, and Bruno Stojic was appointed to an already-defined organ or body, or was it just in the process of getting organised?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in April, with the start of the war in Bosnia, that the defence system started to get organised.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Well, if I understand you correctly, the contours did exist, but the system was still being built up.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the system was still being built up.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, in my set of documents, and I know you're familiar with them also - we needn't waste time on them - but, anyway, in the proposal for the programme of the Defence Department, which is document P 646, dated the 24th of October, 1992, that document speaks about the fact that the activities of the Main Staff, as part of the Defence Department, will be geared towards the constitution of brigades, the setting up of brigades, and their commands, and that is borne out, Mr. Marijan -- or that bears out your theory that the system was still a burgeoning one, under construction?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps they were on to the second phase.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, in document P 128, which is a report on the work -- on work for 1992, at the end of the fifth page and the beginning of page 6, it says, in both versions, Croatian and B/C/S, that -- and English, that after the decision of the 17th of October, 1992, on joining all the Croatian communities in BH into the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, that all the armed units of the HVO came under the united command of the Main Staff. That assertion on the establishment of a united command in mid-October 1992, does that confirm this theory that the system of defence in 1992 was just beginning to be built up?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the system was being built up, and this relates to the Operative Zone of Bosanska Posavina, and only then did it come within the composition of the Main Staff or, rather, the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, document P 661, which is a decision by Mate Boban on the appointment of commanders of the operative zones, dated the 28th of October, 1992. Can we conclude, therefore, that it was in October and during 1992 that the appointments of commanders was an ongoing process to the operative zones and other units of the HVO; is that right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is right. The three men, gentlemen, were appointed because two operative zones had been functioning previously without commanders having been appointed.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Do I still have one more minute at my disposal, with your indulgence, Your Honours? No, I don't? Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have one minute left.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have to complete my cross-examination, Mr. Marijan, unfortunately. Ah, I have been given a minute, right. I have one extra minute.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, in item 8 of your report, that is to say, at the very beginning, you speak about an introductory presentation by my client, Mr. Petkovic. The document is P 279, an introductory speech by my client, Mr. Petkovic. We handed this out to everybody this morning. And, Mr. Marijan, you say that with that speech, the defence priorities of Herceg-Bosna were defined, do you remember that, in paragraph 8 of your report?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it sets out the defence priorities. They weren't defined, however.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, this introductory speech, was it actually delivered? Was this speech uttered and delivered?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't claim that.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, you say that it was a meeting in Grude; right? How do you know that the meeting was held in Grude?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I assume that on the basis of the title, the heading.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: And what does the heading mean, "The Command of the Battle-Field" and so on? It was a forward command post.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was a forward command post. And the command of the southern front at Grude. The southern front was -- there was a unit of the Croatian army, but Mr. Petkovic signed it as a -- the commander of the of this area of Grude and of the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: As commander of the Main Staff, as chief of the Main Staff?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Did you see documents to the effect that as he was brigadier at the time, Brigadier Petkovic signed himself as chief of the Main Staff of the HVO; are you quite sure about that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there are documents, I have documents as commander, not chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, this definition of Grude here, does it mean that in Grude, it was this, the Command of the southern front was there?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was the Forward Command Post.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: So this definition of Grude doesn't actually mean that the meeting was held in Grude, does it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, possibly the meeting was not held in Grude.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Let us assume that the speech was delivered and he is addressing the heads of the municipalities. Tell us which municipalities.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there's several municipalities listed here, probably the municipalities of Western Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: All right, fine. Now, tell me, please, what happened at the end of June 1992 in Western Herzegovina, on that -- in that area there?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the end of June, that is to say, the second half of June 1992, in Western Herzegovina what was happening was this: The HVO had crossed the Neretva River and set up a line on the east bank of the Neretva River; that is to say, Mostar, Capljina, and Stolac municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Tell us, and is that when Stolac was liberated?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, at that same time, the army of Croats and Muslims in Bosnia-Herzegovina --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, you really must conclude, because you really have gone beyond the allotted time.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that mention is made of the enemy in this document, let's try and define it. Were the enemies the army of the Serbs in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: In May 1992?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in May --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: In June 1992, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Those were the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Here it says: "South-east Herzegovina, the Muslims and Croats collaborated"; right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, right.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: Now, from the priorities defined here, and they are --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, Madam, this will be your last question. You really have overstepped the limits.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... it was the professionalisation, as it says -- yes, my last question, here it comes. Defining defence priorities, the professionalisation of the army as being one, the status of HVO members, records kept for everybody participating in the war, and care and attention to the wounded and the families of killed persons, housing -- et cetera. Now -- or, rather, not "et cetera." Are those the defence priorities if you considered that the war had already ended, that war had ended in a given territory; would that be right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Mr. Petkovic says that there are soldiers who consider that the war was already over.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: But I'm asking you about defence priorities here, just your comments on defence priorities, which was my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, Madam Alaburic. The Chamber has been flexible. We gave you an additional five minutes. Really, you must keep to the five minutes, because otherwise there's a boomerang effect. When someone else asks for additional time, the Judges are reticent to grant additional time. So you do understand, I'm sure, the risks involved in our granting additional time, because there's always a risk of slippage. And, frankly, I don't think there's any need to continue. The Chamber therefore decides that this will be the end of your examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... well, if you will, that's fine, if that would be all right with the Trial Chamber. If not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will allow the witness to answer, but you will ask no further questions, please. Go ahead, Witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they are and they're not. Now, professionalisation, if you're going to talk about the professionalisation of the army, it means the war isn't over yet.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Marijan, thank you for your answers. I have no more time left, and therefore I have to complete my cross-examination. I would like to thank the honourable Trial Chamber, and I ask that the Petkovic Defence should be treated equally, just like the Defences of Bruno Stojic and some other Defence teams, when Mr. Karnavas presented his evidence. So thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, there is a question that should have been asked to you, based on the document we have before us, where there is a breakdown of the military personnel, Mostar, Capljina, Grude, Stolac, et cetera. When I add up the numbers, it comes to about 10.000 soldiers. And a few days ago, I saw another document where I did a similar addition. And when I was doing that, I wondered what the HVO represented on the ground in terms of military force. Just a few thousand soldiers, whereas we know that on the other side -- well, I'm not going to speak about the Serb side, but -- because we're essentially interested here in the Muslim side. They were far more numerous. You, yourself, were on the ground. You were in the field, and you said that you fought. Did you have the impression that you were out-numbered, that there was an imbalance in terms of military personnel, weaponry, and military force? Did you have the impression that you were on equal footing with the other side or were you in a situation of inferiority, number-wise?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, the Bosnian Serbian army, or rather the Serbian army in Bosnia-Herzegovina, took over all the capacities of the Yugoslav People's Army, all their facilities, so in this specific case on the opposite bank of the Neretva River, there was a corps that was pulled out of Croatia from the area of Istria and Rijeka, and so the corps was an establishment corps with three brigades, an anti-aircraft team, an artillery regiment, and all the elements that a corps has. Now, the overall HVO did not have the necessary resources to amount to one corps, and then there was the human problem as well. The Serbs during this period were facing a lot of confusion. In the summer of 1992 itself, they managed to consolidate themselves in July with additional mobilisations, so their supremacy, both in manpower and technical equipment, was constant; whereas with the Muslims, they had superiority in manpower, and this could be seen on the ground, they had more men, the Muslims were more numerous; although, just like the HVO, they didn't have support which would correspond to the number of manpower.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question, and then I will call upon the Stojic Defence. Given the number of soldiers and presence that you've just described, how can it be that the HVO and its military component was not simply wiped away? Why weren't they just swept away very rapidly? I mean in military terms, of course.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Your Honour, that is indeed a question, and the same question can be asked of Croatia, because it took one of the JNA's corps, the 17th corps, but it did manage to resist an attack. And I suppose that it came down to the human factor, especially on the Serb side. The human factor was not on a par with the weapons, on the same level as their level of armament. That's the only explanation, I think, because morale was the decisive factor, and the will to fight. That was the decisive factor in all these conflicts, and it was the source of all the successes and failures of any one of those armies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps we'll have an opportunity to come back to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, your previous answer, towards the end, features your assessment that while the Muslims were in a majority as far as people, men, are concerned, they lacked support. If one has a minimum knowledge of military and war, one knows that it's mainly fire that is important, more than legs, so wouldn't that be an explanation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, no. I can quote a specific example, if you would like me to do that, so that I back up what would otherwise just be my story, a tale told by me. On the 13th of April, 1992, for example - this is a specific case, and I can quote that - I was along a sector that was 13 kilometres long, a line defended by 350 men. We had -- of heavy weaponry, we had one non-recoilless gun - it's a small one - 80 millimetres, two mortars of 120 millimetres, and apart from those of us who were outside the local structures, there was a group of volunteers from the Croatian Army, some 30 men in all, and they also had two mortars of 120 millimetres, and there was another group of 20 or 30 men of the Croatian Party of Rights, the HOS group. I think you've already heard about the HOS. Anyway, on that particular day, after intense preparations where our lines were -- artillery preparations, we were attacked by an armoured battalion, about 20 armoured vehicles, mostly tanks, and they didn't manage to break through. So if you look at that and look at some examples -- call examples that would be taught, to all intents and purposes, they would have had to break down our lines, but they didn't, they didn't break down our defence. Although there was a lot of panic and fear, but nonetheless we managed to stick to our guns and hold our positions, so that I think that morale is all important and a basic feature in a war.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much for that example. I would like to call upon Mr. Coric's Defence. You have 30 minutes, in order to avoid any difficulties, 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. Good morning, Mr. Marijan. Good morning to everyone in the courtroom. My questions will refer to certain paragraphs in your report under the heading "Military police."

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: You have the report before you? You must have my documents plus your own report.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 44 of your report, you refer to two documents, and one of them reads that the Military Police Administration leads and commands all military police units, and in the other document it says it commands military police units in units, operation zones, and the light assault brigade. Now, in the follow-up, not because I always want clarifications but because I have very little time, please answer me with a "yes" or "no." Tell me, do you -- have you found this parts of your report and do you remember these documents?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Yesterday and in the previous days of your testimony, you pointed out a problem, or what you see as a problem, in the documents in general enactments of the HVO, and the question was raised in the courtroom whether you were a lawyer, whether you were qualified to comment on these documents, and I took all that into account when I prepared for my cross-examination. And I will follow the example of the Presiding Judge, Mr. Antonetti, and try to focus my examination on very specific issues and what happened in practice. That's why I would like us to look together at a few documents, starting with the last one in your binder, 5D 0 --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please repeat the number.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] While this document is coming up -- 5D 00440.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: I'll remind you that in paragraph 43 of your report, quoting the Decree on the Armed Forces, you said that the military police was charged with security and military traffic, military order and discipline, and elimination of criminal elements in the armed forces. Now, these things that I quoted from your paragraph 3, is this in fact the basic job description of the military police, what they are supposed to do on a daily basis; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Now we have the document on the screen. It's a document signed by the commander, Tihomir Blaskic. Let's see what it says. It's a warning to one of the brigade commanders of the HVO, where he says that the overall status of the military police of the HVO is the responsibility of the brigade commander, and he says further below that the brigade commander is under obligation to prevent all incidents of robbery, crime, and seizure of motor vehicles. Does this fall within the daily tasks of the military police; for instance, the elimination of criminal elements in the armed forces?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Look at the next --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would like to take -- I'd like to take advantage of your looking at this document. I'll ask a question. We have this document signed by Mr. Blaskic. Could you comment on the codes 01-1-425/93? Could you tell us what it means, so we have a specific example.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think you could explain it this way. "01" should be the code of the Operation Zone Central Bosnia. "-1," it means it was signed by the commander of the operation zone, because if it had been the head of the Main Staff, it would have been "02," and other assistants would follow. "425/93" would mean that it is the 425th document written in 1993, which means that in the first nine days of the year, the operations zone had already had 425 different documents developed in its General Affairs Department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Summarising "01," operational area?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "01" is commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. "1" means Colonel Blaskic is in command, and "45" is the 425th document in 1993, date and time. Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I have a small rather linguistic question. The document, in the English translation, mentions "seizure of motor vehicles." Now, "seizure" is a technical/legal term and it doesn't make sense in this context. Isn't car theft or taking cars for joy-riding rather what was meant here?

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the original documents, it says "otimanje," [phoen] that is appropriation, illegal, unlawful appropriation, something that is a crime.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Now, let us move on to document 5D 04384. It's the next one in line, again from Mr. Blaskic, addressed to the 4th Battalion of the Military Police of Vitez. It's a command that is -- it's an order, where it says, "Immediately distribute or deploy confiscated vehicles." Does this fall within the normal job description of the military police?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: 5D 03046 will be our next document. Now, we are moving to the South-East Herzegovina Operational Zone. This document was signed by Commander Bozo Pavlovic. He issues orders to the military police in this document. And if we look at paragraph 1, he stipulates passage through check-points. 5D 03046. Check-points in traffic. Check-points, is that a normal job of the military police?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Let's move on to the next document, 5D 04380, again from Mr. Bozo Pavlovic, again an order to the military police of Stolac, and it concerns the taking into custody and disarmament of those who leave their positions without official leave. Is that one of the jobs of the military police?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Let's move on to the next document. In fact, we can skip it, because we have enough from Operation Zone South-East Herzegovina. We're skipping one. And let's move to 5D 04392. That's another order from Mr. Bozo Pavlovic, addressed to both the civilian and the military police, and again he deals with check-points, orders a ban on the misappropriation of property. Is that another job of the military police?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Next document, 5D 02009. This is an order from the commander of the Sector South, Nedeljko Obradovic. We see down below that it was addressed to the chief of the active police, Dretelj. It's entitled: "Order concerning check-points"; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: 501548, Operation Zone West Herzegovina. It's from commander Zeljko Siljeg, and the title is "Engaging Forces to Execute Military Police Tasks in Gornji Vakuf." Now, in the introductory paragraph of this order, somewhere towards the middle, there is a sentence that reads: "Since the military police, since some time ago, has been subordinated in the command sense to the commands of brigades and operations zones, and with a view to appropriate engagement and establishing order in Gornji Vakuf ...," we need not read the rest, "... he orders brigades Kvaternik and Ante Starcevic to proceed with performing their daily regular tasks." It's document P 01548. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Now, put your finger on this passage. In fact, we can move on with the documents. We'll skip one, and we'll skip the next one. 5D 0201. Leave your finger on 5D 02001. In your report, you said that the military police had been engaged from the very beginning in combat operations; am I right?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Now, with regard to these combat activities, I'd like to look at certain documents. Let's look at document 5D 04371. Can you see it? It's the first one after the one where you left your finger. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: We see that this is an order from Commander Zvonko Vukovic. He's the commander of the 4th Battalion of the Military Police in Vitez, and he addresses this order to all military police units in the Central Bosnia Operation Zone. He says: "Pursuant to the order of the HVO Main Staff," number such and such, "and further to the order of the Operations Zone Central Bosnia," and he gives an order to raise command readiness in all the military police units. Is this the chain of command in the combat operations involving military police?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: 5D 04382 is the next document I need. It's an order from the commander of the Operations Zone South-East Herzegovina, Mr. Milenko Lazic, sent to the military police, among others, and in para 3 it says that an anti-aircraft machine-gun should be mounted on the military police vehicle. Does this order relate to the supply of a certain weapon to the military police in connection with an operation?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: The next document, P 03117, again from the commander of the Operation Zone South-East Herzegovina, Brigadier Milenko Lazic, addressed to the 3rd Battalion of the Military Police, and it says: "Pursuant to the order from the Main Staff, specifying the responsibilities of the operation zone in stabilising the situation," and he goes on. And I'd like to look at item 2 -- paragraph 2, the point that begins with the second zone of responsibility. He describes the location and he says: "I appoint Mr. Mijo Jelic, sector commander," and in brackets "commander of the military police." Now let's look at item 4. It says daily reports in writing, describing the situation as of 1800 hours, to be submitted by sector commanders and telephone reports to be submitted, et cetera, et cetera. Does this reflect the chain of command over the military police in combat operations?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Now, one document we'll skip. 5D 04385 is the next document I need. It's an order from Colonel Zeljko Siljeg, sent to the 2nd Battalion of the Military Police in Livno, among others, entitled: "Reporting to the Command of the Operation Zone North-East Herzegovina." In para 1, Mr. Siljeg [Livenote read in error "Zilic"] says: "The 2nd Military Police Battalion ..." and he enumerates other units that are not of interest to me, "... shall be required to submit regular combat reports on the situation as of 1800 hours by 1900 hours every day, and interim reports as needed. Send reports in writing using a courier or pact communications." I have just been warned by my colleague that we have "Zilic" instead of "Siljeg" in the transcript. It's Commander Siljeg. Is this the structure of orders received by the military police?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we could conclude that this unit is involved in combat.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: 5D 04387 is the next document. I think it's a combat order again signed by Zeljko Siljeg, and it's called "Order for Active Combat Activity." Look at para 2. In para 2 of the order, it says "Tactical Group 2." Now, look at its composition, please. Among others, we see the military police. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: And it says, Tactical Group 2 has the mission to launch an attack on enemy forces from line such and such. Now, let us look at para 8 of the same order, where it says the 2nd Military Police Battalion, and he lists others, shall move on the axis of operation of Tactical Group 2, and describes that mission in that operation. Remember that we have the 2nd Battalion of Military Police in para 8, and let's see to whom this order was addressed. Addressees, units from para 8. Tell me, is this a combat order sent to the military police?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to go back to the document I told you to put a finger on, P -- 5D 02001. Look at point 3 of that document. It's once again a Zeljko Siljeg document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, you said something on the evaluation, the assessment of the forces in presence, and I can see here from this document that there are T-55 tanks. Have you heard what I said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, T-55. I did hear that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No comment on this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, a tank platoon is mentioned there, which means two or three tanks at the most. To be quite honest, I didn't understand. Did you say something before? I just heard you say "T-55 tanks," but I didn't hear what you said before that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I said, we had a discussion earlier on, on the assessment of forces in presence, and after what you said, I just point out to you that the paragraph in question states that there were some tanks available to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, without a doubt the HVO had tanks, but the overall HVO in all three zones, well, I think the figures exist, but I don't think that the Operative Zone had more than 10 or 12 tanks, the whole of the Operative Zone. So just two or three are used to reinforce the infantry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. It was a minor issue.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: And to conclude this area with respect to the combat operations, let's look at the documents P 02001 [as interpreted] and item 3 of that. It is a Siljeg document in which he says that the general principle was that the unit, who was the strongest establishment-wise and is to be found in a given territory, at a given time, should command all the other units in that territory, and this is regulated by an order from the superior commander. 5D 02001 is the document number, 5D. So it commands all the units on the territories, and this is regulated by the order issued by the superior commander. Now, do you agree with what Colonel Siljeg writes there, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is the general principle of a commander on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: All right, fine. Let's move on to the first document in my binder now. And we can go to the last page of that document or, rather, paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Hold on. There may be legal consequences for that principle in paragraph 3. You're not a lawyer - we know that - but I'm asking you this question because you were in the field. According to this document, it would seem that when, in the field, automatically a stronger unit subordinates all the other units present in the field, is it how this paragraph is to be understood? Because then I would have another question ensuing from your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise, but I think there was a mistake in the interpretation, because it says that you said that that strongest one was subordinated to all the rest, whereas I think you meant to say that it was superior to all the others. There was a mistake in the translation of your words into Croatian and English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have understood, but since the French interpreters are excellent, there's never any problem. I have understood that it is the stronger unit which has authority over all the other units on the ground. Is this what this text means?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The principle is that the largest unit or, rather, the commander of the largest unit commands the forces attached to him on the ground, because that is how to avoid multiple chains of command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Assuming that, let us imagine the following hypothesis. Well, it's actually not a hypothesis; it was the reality. We have seen this. But for you, it would be a hypothesis. Imagine the military police unit, who's not from the brigade but from other brigades, i.e., it comes from elsewhere, imagine that unit is in the field. Is it automatically subordinated to the unit which in the field is the strongest one, and is that military police unit subordinated to the commander of that stronger unit? So it's a very specific point.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Its very entry, entry of that unit, into the zone of a bigger unit, brings it into that position, and in most cases there should be an additional document from the commander who sent the unit there to avoid any possible queries in that sense.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So this outside unit is placed under the authority of the commander exercising the main authority? Are we in agreement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, precisely, Your Honour, quite right.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Well, let's take the first document in my binder now. It is about the military police and its establishment. You've referred to that many times, and so have we all in the court. So let's move to the last page, and you can recall the documents we showed a moment ago related to daily assignments. And let's read the penultimate paragraph of that document, in which it says that the commanders of the military police battalions in operation zones, in performing their daily duties, are directly subordinated to the operation zone commander and carry out all orders relating to military police work and assignments, in accordance with the powers and responsibilities of the military police. That is document, let me repeat again, P 00957. Now, what I've just read out, is that in keeping with the orders we looked at a moment ago about check-points, law and order, the documents I showed you a moment ago; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: All right. Now I'd like to read out a sentence. This is a bit confusing, and then another document, so that we can clear up what that actually means, because I would like to draw a conclusion about what it is, in actual fact, that the military police does. And in this same document, one sentence before the part I read out, says, "The Military Police Administration leads and commands all military police units." Remember that sentence, please. Now, in the binder, find P 00143 now, P 00143 is the document you should be looking at now. It's a document to which you refer in paragraph 24. Have you found it?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: And after that, there's a later document, a subsequent document, P 00837 by another author, and it comes next in my binder. I'm just going to read out the P 00143 document because they are identical in the portion that interests me. So let's look at general provisions, Chapter 1 in that document. Let me help out Your Honours and tell you where it is in the English. It is on page 4, page 4 of the English. Have you found Chapter 1, Witness?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Now, in Chapter 1, we have something under number 1, and what you said is quoted there; that the Military Police Administration shall lead all the military police units. And I showed you a document linked to daily operations, combat operations. Now, in that same document, under item 9 -- let's look at paragraphs 9 and 11 and see what the author of the document tells us there. 9 and 11, please. In point 9, the author of the document says as follows: "The Military Police Administration of the HVO is responsible for the general situation, professional training, and combat readiness of the military police units. "It shall monitor and study the organisation and formation of military police units and control and evaluate the level of training and combat readiness of military police units, and the HVO shall propose measures for their improvement and replenishment. "The Military Police Administration shall also draw conclusions from experiences gained in the work of the military police units and incorporate them into the training of the military police units." Let's look at paragraph 11 now, please. 11 paragraph, which says the following: "The Military Police Administration is responsible for equipping the military police units with military police equipment and insignia showing that they belong to military police units, while for the armament and providing other materiel and technical equipment, it is the command of the basic unit that is responsible for that, attached to which the military police unit has been formed." Paragraph 11. Now, I have two questions, in conclusion. What I've just read out, paragraphs 9 and 11, that is, do they explain the way in which and the sense in which all the military police units are commanded by the Military Police Administration and what the Military Police Administration is responsible for; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: Now, my last question, and I will conclude my cross-examination with that question: Can I therefore conclude that when, in paragraph 37 of your report, in the last sentence there, you state - take a look at paragraph 37 now, please - that the military police was treated as part of the armed forces. When you say that, do you mean the military police units, in fact, and not the Military Police Administration, which is the administrative part of the Defence department; am I right there? And that's my last question.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, that completes my cross-examination. I would just like to mention, I don't know whether this was clear enough yesterday, but Ms. Alaburic showed schematics yesterday. Well, they weren't schematics that were compiled during the war; they were schematics drawn up during these proceedings, during this trial, and there are some which are not contradictory to those dating back to the war. So when we present our evidence during the Coric Defence case, we shall be showing those, too. Thank you, Your Honours, and thank you, Mr. Marijan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. That comment is, of course, included in the transcript, and the Chamber will take account of it. Thank you very much for having concluded your examination. You used up your 30 minutes, more or less, and that will enable us, therefore, to have a 20-minute break now. And then the Prosecution can begin its cross-examination. Twenty minutes' break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I call upon the Prosecution, I would like to read out a brief decision on the part of the Chamber regarding the appearance of Slobodan Bozic. The appearance of Slobodan Bozic, a witness for the Stojic Defence, is planned January 26 to February 3rd, 2009. In keeping with the schedule presented by the Stojic Defence, they have asked for five hours in order to carry out the direct examination. On December 16th, 2008, the Praljak Defence had requested the time of 15 to 20 minutes during the appearance of Slobodan Bozic in order to carry out a direct examination of this same witness under Article 92 ter of the Rules. On January 12th, 2009, the Praljak Defence indicated to the Chamber and to the parties -- or, rather, disclosed to the Chamber and to the parties the English translation of the written statement made by Slobodan Bozic which they intend to present in keeping with Article 92 ter of the Rules. On January 16th, 2009, the Prosecution responded that they were not opposed to the request made by the Praljak Defence to carry out direct examination of this witness, while requesting to have additional time for its own cross-examination. The Chamber grants the request made by the Praljak Defence to carry out a direct examination of Slobodan Bozic under Article 92 ter of the Rules, and decides, in keeping with the practice of the Chamber, to grant the following amount of time: First of all, the Stojic Defence shall have five hours in order to carry out the direct examination of the witness Slobodan Bozic. The other Defence teams will have an overall amount of time of two and a half hours, two hours and thirty minutes, for their cross-examination, and the Prosecution will then be able to cross-examine the witness for a duration of five hours. Secondly, the Praljak Defence will have 20 minutes for the direct examination of the witness, in keeping with Article 92 ter of the Rules. The other Defence teams will have an overall amount of time of 15 minutes, and the Prosecution 30 minutes for cross-examination of the witness in relationship to the direct examination carried out by the Praljak Defence and on the basis of the written statement of the witness. So to summarise, we will have five hours for the Stojic Defence team. All the other teams will have two and a half hours, and then the Prosecutor will have five hours. Then Mr. Praljak will have 20 minutes, the other Defence teams 15 minutes, and the Prosecutor 30 minutes. I therefore have summarised the situation in just a few seconds. Mr. Karnavas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just a point of clarification, Mr. President and Your Honours. Are we to understand, then, that there will be no cross-examination on the part of the Praljak team? Because it seems that they're both doing direct and cross under this -- as the way the order is stated. First they cross and then they do direct? Because I understand initially they had requested both direct and cross-examination time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Based on what Mr. Praljak requested in his submission, he will have the opportunity to cross-examine within the overall time of two and a half hours. And once we've completed all of that, he will then come back, under Article 92 ter, to deal with the issues in that statement. Have you understood?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I do understand. I just find it rather interesting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may, it's not the first time that we have this. We've had it with your witnesses, too. And we have developed that. No one objected to the system and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I did believe -- I did note that I found it rather curious. I didn't -- it's not my position to object to somebody else's demands at this point in time with respect to cross and direct, although I do find it interesting. On the one moment, he's hostile or being treated as a hostile witness, and the next moment you're embracing him as your own witness. But be that as it may, I accept Trial Chamber's decision, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: We will not discuss now all the curiosities that are associated to this trial because that might take some time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Indeed, it would take numerous days. Mr. Bos, you have the floor now. Thank you very much, because we do have a file.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours, and everybody else in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Marijan. Yes, you have a lot of binders around you piled up. All the binders from the Defence, I think, you can leave now. Please keep them on the ground. What's important is your report, which I think you have in front of you, your expert report, and those two binders that are actually right here. Mr. Marijan, I will deal with a number of topics, but before I do, I'd like to make -- ask you for a couple of clarifications on your report. And for that, I would ask you to go to your introductory remarks on page 4 of your report, the introductory remarks. Do you have that? In those introductory remarks, you make reference -- well, you talk in the plural, you say: "Our intention was to present the organisation and volume of work and task carried out by the Department of Defence." And in the third paragraph, again, you say: "A major obstacle in our work was a lack of clear information ..." Et cetera. Now, who do you refer to besides yourself when you say "our"?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's a normal usage in my profession, shared by most of my colleagues, to say "we," "our." You can find it in all of my books. Some people say "I," but I always wrote "we." I don't think I can explain. I simply took it over from others. It's regular usage.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Does it in any way imply that other people were involved in the preparation of this report besides you?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is my report, Mr. Bos. I signed it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And you signed it, and whatever is written in the report has been written by you?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by it, yes. Yes, I wrote it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did you read everything in the report?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote all of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, did you get compensated for writing this report?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: You didn't get any compensation. And did you write this report in your free time or did you prepare it --

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was done in my spare time.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, from the cross by other counsel, it appears that you reviewed a substantial number of documents, and I would like to clarify the documents that you actually reviewed.
