Did you review -- let me first ask you this: Did you review more documents than the documents you've been [sic] footnoted in your report?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And when you say "certainly," can you give an estimate on the number of documents that you actually reviewed? Are we talking about hundreds of more documents or --

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure you know that I used to work as the archivist who laid the foundations for this. A lot of documents passed through my hands. And when I say "a lot," that's what I mean, a great, great deal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: But when -- when you start preparing for this report, were all the documents that you reviewed, were they all given to you by the Stojic Defence or did they give part of the documents and you also referred to documents that you had already written before or that you already had in your possession, yourself?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I used the documents I received from the Stojic Defence team and your documents, I believe, because they bear a Prosecution reference number. And in my research, I had access to material, additional material that I used. I don't know if their exhibit number was given them later or was already there when I reviewed them. I didn't pay attention.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What I would like to find out is -- so you say that you were also given Prosecution exhibits. Do you know what kind of selection the Stojic Defence made in providing you these documents? Did they give you the complete Prosecution exhibit list or additional documents as well? Do you know what kind of selection they made for you -- for the documents for you to review?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Stojic Defence gave me access to the documents they had, and I was given a topic, a subject. And according to that subject, I reviewed documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: When you say "they had," well, let's be concrete, for example. Did you get the full Prosecution exhibit list with all the documents from the Prosecution exhibits list, or a number of the Prosecution exhibits?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you if that was all or some of them. I must say I wasn't particularly interested. It was a great number of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay, very well. Let's move to paragraph 17 of your report, and that's on page 13 of at least the English version. This paragraph 17 talks about the role of the Department of Defence, and there I'll pick out one line from this paragraph. You quote it, you said: "The Department of Defence of the HVO was based on a Western European model, with practice of civilian supervision of the army." Now, sir, in most -- and you've touched upon this issue already in cross-examination by Ms. Alaburic, but so in most Western countries, the defence minister is charged with both formulating the defence policy and executing this policy by providing the necessary direction and support to the armed forces. Is it not true did Mr. Stojic had a similar de jure role in the HVO Department of Defence?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, this evaluation I made is based on the practice that I know. I can't say that I dealt with and studied in detail with Western practices. I studied them only through the bulletins published by the army. I don't know if that was the custom in the past or even now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... because you yourself are quoting the Western European model, so I would think that you have an idea of what the Western European model entails. And isn't it true, sir, that it, in fact, means that the defence minister is actually formulating defence policy and is executing this policy by providing direction and support to the armed forces? That's usually how it works in Western -- in Western countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I will object to the testifying. I mean, I don't know if the gentleman is an expert or has served as a minister of defence in the West, whatever "Western" means.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, I'm just asking him his interpretation of the Western European model, and that's what he's referring to --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: The gentleman is testifying, and there's a vast difference between how the Secretary of Defence in the United States conducts himself versus somebody, say, in France or England or elsewhere, so I would object to any testifying.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sir, what is your interpretation of -- when you refer to the Western European model, what -- how did you consider the role of the defence minister?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I understand the role of minister in that model as a person who is not in the chain of command and who is a civilian. And the army, the Main Staff, is directly looking to the Supreme Commander. I believe I said that already. And the fundamental call for a civilian society that arose in the 1980s in the former Yugoslavia, primarily in Slovenia, resulted in a call for the defence minister to be a civilian. I believe that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: If the minister of defence was a civilian, then the next question is: Would he have, as a civilian, control over the HVO defence army?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. I did not intervene several times yesterday, but I only noticed it by reviewing the transcript. The full answer of the witness is not recorded. The witness said, in his answer on page 49, line 20 -- he added: "But Yugoslavia was peculiar and the JNA was peculiar, idiosyncratic," and that was not recorded, whereas it qualifies his answer. He said it was a peculiar, idiosyncratic model, and that was not recorded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did say that. And when I'm speaking about this, Mr. Prosecutor, this entire paragraph reflects the ambition, the striving. That's how they perceived, from their perspective, not only of the Croats of Herceg-Bosna; they perceived that the minister of defence is not a military man and is not part of the chain of command, and that was the great novelty compared to the JNA. The JNA, I believe, was against --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: But what I'm now asking is you -- to you is: Was there civilian control over the military?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there has been discussion about that in the past days. We have this problem of the political organisation in Herceg-Bosna, which I admit is very difficult for me to understand. On the one hand, we have this Presidency of the HZ-HB consisting of presidents of municipalities, and they are on the third step. And based on that, we have my conclusion from what I saw in the documents that their influence and supervision over the army was great at that lower level. Now, you can ask the question whether such influence was desirable at a higher level, but the HVO overall was not a problematic army in that sense. Of course, you have the war, which is always a peculiar situation, leading to militarisation and less civilian control.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I understand what you said. You said that also yesterday. And let me repeat to you again, because you're now talking about on a lower level, there was civilian control, rather than on a higher level. But yesterday, when you were asked by Ms. Alaburic the following question, and I'll quote from page 93 of yesterday's transcript, the question was: "So, in principle, what are the instruments of the civilian control over the military?" And then you answered: "Well, when we are talking about the HZ-HB, the civilian control was meant to be in the hands of the HVO, and it was meant to be in the hands of Mr. Stojic. This is what I talked about yesterday or the day before." Isn't that what you said, Mr. Marijan?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it's on the record, then I probably did say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yes or no would suffice, Mr. Marijan. I'm asking you whether you said it, and you actually did say it. Now, let me ask you -- and this morning again we went back to this transcript for Mr. Tudjman. What I'm interested in is: Why did you quote Mr. Tudjman as an authority for interpreting what the role of the minister of defence was in the Herceg-Bosna government? What made you choose Mr. Tudjman as an authority?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I am rather familiar with the biography of Mr. Tudjman, and this is perhaps a curious digression in the former Yugoslavia. There was a 30-year-long discussion, debate, about command and control that we are discussing here, and he was the first person who started it back in 1953. I believe he is extremely qualified, militarily speaking. And regardless of the fact that he left active military service early in the 1960s, he kept thinking as a military man, as a soldier, and he was very well acquainted with the arrangements within the JNA, and he was obviously trying to depart from that in creating the Croatian system.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: But did it maybe have anything to do with the fact that Tudjman had some sort of control over what was happening in Herceg-Bosna? Would that maybe have been a reason also for you to quote Mr. Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, the influence of Mr. Tudjman on Herceg-Bosna is indisputable. It cannot be questioned. We can see that from the large number of transcripts that I had the occasion to read. I cannot be certain about the degree of his supervision, though.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, sir, having reviewed all these documents and these various transcripts, isn't it true that that -- actually, that the Herceg-Bosna government took directions from Mr. Tudjman?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some sessions, yes, this was discussed. I would rather say that it was Tudjman's relationship with Mr. Boban, first of all. Then there were other members of Herceg-Bosna attending these sessions. Whether you can view this as directions or not, I think you have among your exhibits the transcript of his conversation with Boban, where Tudjman and Susak suggest to him that he should withdraw from his position, and from the same transcript you can conclude that this supervision is not really that great. In fact, it's difficult to evaluate it. In my opinion, if there had been full supervision, we wouldn't be discussing -- they would not be discussing it at all. They would just tell Boban, "It's time for you to go." From this conversation, you can see that Herceg-Bosna enjoyed great independence, but of course that's my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we'll leave that topic and --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: -- let me know ask you -- I'm getting the French translation in my earphones here. Again on the civilian supervision, Mr. Marijan, yesterday when you were cross-examined by Madam Alaburic, you agreed with her that the HVO civil authorities had instruments such an finance, procurement, and security control at their disposal to control the military, but then you also claimed that such control was much more obvious at the local municipal level than rather at the higher level; is that correct? Is that what you were saying?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: It just requires a yes-or-no answer. And is it correct that as an example of this more local municipal control, you testified on Monday that municipalities in Herceg-Bosna often financed their own defence?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw that in some documents, and I know a specific case that I saw myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Yeah, you gave the specific example of Livno, where you claimed that the Livno Brigade, which is the Kresimir 4th Brigade, was actually paid by the Livno municipalities until at least, you say, October/November 1993; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the Livno Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I'm going to show you two exhibits now. The first one is P 09551, and it's not in the binder, but it's in the bundle that's on top of the binder, the separate bundle. Could you please look at that? Yes, it's that bundle, right, yes, and it's the -- it has two exhibits, and I'm interested in the second one, P 09551. And this is an activity report of the HVO of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. And what I'm particularly interested in, in this document, is it contains a budget for the year 1993, and it's -- in the B/C/S version, there's numbers on the bottom of the pages, and you have to go to page 0040-5235. And for the English, it's on page 42 and 43, Your Honours. So, Mr. Marijan, what we have here is a budget of the HVO, Herceg-Bosna, for the year 1993, and you first see the budget revenue, and that budget revenue totals an amount which is -- I think it's billion, 2.17 billion Croatian dinar. Can you see that? It's the total of the revenue, and it's an amount of 217.772.972.774 [sic] billion, or trillion. Page 40? Yes, for the e-court, it's page 40, the B/C/S version. Do you see that, Mr. Marijan?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, Mr. Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And then so what follows is the budget expenditure, and what I would like to focus your attention to is the expenditure -- the money that actually goes to the Ministry of Defence. It's -- if you compare it with the other ministries, it's an amount of 169 billion Croatian dinars, and would you agree with me, sir, that it's -- that if you look at what is going to the other departments, that the Ministry of Defence is getting the main chunk of money? Would you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this figure is obviously the biggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: In fact, it's -- I've made a calculation, and it's almost 78 per cent of the total budget that goes actually to the Ministry of Defence. Now, if you would put this amount of money against the financial resources that the municipalities had at their disposal, would you agree that whatever the municipalities had at their disposal was peanuts against what the HVO Defence Department had at their disposal for finance?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to admit that, well, I'm not really well-versed in this subject. It is a large number, and why isn't it in -- if it were in German marks, I would be better able to respond, but it's difficult for me to say since it's in Croatian dinars. But I'm not an expert in this matter. To the best of my recollections is this: that we were paid by the municipalities, the salaries, that is, without going into other matters, and this caused a hullabaloo, if I can put it that way. Well, they weren't large salaries. When I was a student, it would have been like pocket money, decent pocket money. So how a family with two children could live on that, I don't know. But the fact remains that it is a lot of money.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: But -- and would you agree with me, you agree that it's --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, but I have to intervene here. My learned friend Mr. Bos is asking the expert whether it's a large sum in relation to what the municipalities have. Now, let him show us where, in the budget, we have stated how much the municipalities have. The municipalities have their own budget. This is just for the HZ-HB, HVO HZ-HB. There's no budget for the municipalities here at all. And as the witness says that he's not a financial expert, I think that this is just adding confusion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, let me just make this point, and regardless of what kind of budget the municipalities had. Would you agree that if the HVO Defence Department had such large amounts of money at their disposal, that it would make them powerful towards the local municipalities?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: I'm going to object. I'm going to object to the form of the question, Your Honour. Again, and I was about to object earlier, we don't know what the municipalities have and have not, and there are various municipalities. It all depends on where they're located and whether they have a large number of people in the diaspora. So that question cannot be answered, not by this particular gentleman, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos, in order to avoid constant objections from the Defence, which may use up time, and since we're all seeking the truth, and since we are all trying to know what happened within the chain of command, when you ask your questions, please lay first the foundations and say, for example, "In the municipalities of Bosnia-Herzegovina, there were such and such situations," and then you follow on, in order to avoid any objection on the time scope, the geographical scope, because your question may not fall into the scope. So by your question, please start setting the scope, time, time-wise, and space-wise, so that the Defence will not be entitled to raising objections. You see, when I ask questions of the witness, I said, "You were in that unit at that," et cetera, et cetera, so I set the question in a particular background so that there is no possible objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: And, Your Honour, just to follow up on your observations, if we had looked at P 00588, which is a document cited by the gentleman, which was covered on both direct and cross, it's the Decree on the Armed Forces, and it is dated 17 October 1992, Article 170, which apparently was omitted to be commented on in full, it says here: "Funding of the Armed Forces of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna shall be carried out according to the budget of the Defence Department, adopted by member municipalities of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna." And then it goes on about the contributions. And my point is this: If the gentleman wishes to pursue this line of questioning, and perhaps this should have been done in the expertise, at a minimum there should be some proof of what the municipalities' budget was pursuant to Article 170, assuming that they did comply with this particular decision or decree. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You can move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I'll move on to the next exhibit, and that's Exhibit P 10674, and for that you'll need the binder, Mr. Marijan. You can put that aside.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, while you are finding this exhibit, it's P 10674, I'll tell you what the document is. This document is a compilation of various documents relating to the financial support of the Croatian Ministry of Defence to the HVO. And, Your Honours, I think I've seen this document before. It's been also shown to another witness. It's P 10674. It's the yellow tab. As I said, Mr. Marijan, it's a compilation of various orders, and, for example, if I take you first maybe to the second order, the order dated the 29th of October, 1992, this is from Mr. Susak to the Financial Administration, and it says: "I order 83 million Croatian dinars from the funds of the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Croatia to be loaned to the HVO. The money is strictly intended for the 2nd Stolac Battalion and the Neum Battalion." And then it continues: "The money order should be immediately paid into the account number ... in Zagreb." And it's signed by Mr. Susak. And so we have a number of those orders, and the one I'd like you now to look at is the order dated the 10th of January, 1993, and it's the fifth order, I think. This, in fact, is not from Mr. Susak, but this is a document from Mr. Stojic addressed to the Defence Ministry in Croatia, and it's a list of salaries for the officers of soldiers in Herceg-Bosna for the period December 1992. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, so we see a whole list of units and brigades being mentioned there, and please look at, under number 30, there it says: "The Kresimir 4th Brigade Command," and then there's an amount of 2.971.450 dinar being requested by Mr. Stojic for this particular command unit for salaries. Now, sir, doesn't this contradict what you said in your testimony, that the Livno Brigade, to your knowledge, never -- that the Municipality of Livno actually paid the salaries of this brigade up 'til November 1993?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, I know for sure that the municipality -- no -- well, did pay out, during the period of time I was there, that is to say, from 1992, the summer of 1992, until September 1992, while I was there, and from July or several months in 1993. I do know that the municipality did provide this. Whether anybody else took part, I don't know. And to be quite honest, it's difficult for me to find my way here, because there are a lot of -- big differences in the sums. The 1st Herzegovina Brigade in 1992, for example, which is a little larger than the Kresimir 4th Brigade, has almost 12 times more money. So translated into -- according to the German mark exchange rate, it's not a lot of money; that is to say, there are big differences particularly between that particular brigade and, as I say, the Livno Brigade, and they had a similar number of men. So I don't know -- but I can't say whether that was enough for a salary or whether the salaries were sufficient. Just look at how much the professional units were paid on the next page. Companies received far more money than some brigades, for example --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: But, Mr. Marijan --

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- so it's a very small sum.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: -- that's not the point I'm trying to make here. Regardless of what kind of money was given to whom, isn't it true that money was being also given to the --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for getting to my feet again, but I'd like to ask that the entire witness answer be recorded. He said that it is a very small sum of money, so may we have the whole answer recorded, which means, Mr. Marijan, could you speak up, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, Ms. Nozica has made an important point. It is difficult to record what you say perhaps because you do not speak loudly enough, and so please speak loudly. And when you feel that what you say is important, please stress it so that it's properly and duly recorded. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do my best, Your Honour. Mr. Bos, without a doubt, looking at this, part of the money did reach the Defence Ministry. That's what you wanted to hear; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay, let's move on, Mr. Marijan. Let me refer back to your report, to paragraph 6 of your report. I'm going to put to you a couple of quotes from your report concerning the role of the Ministry of Defence, where it concerns logistics. And in paragraph 6 of your report, you state: "Article 41," and you're referring to the Decree on the Armed Forces, "stipulates that the Department of Defence will be in charge of supplying the armed forces with combat equipment (weapons, artillery pieces, ammunition) while the supply of the armed forces with material, equipment, food, funds, medical, veterinarian and other supplies will be carried out by the Department of Defence in cooperation with other departments of the HVO, as well as other institutions and bodies." And then moving to paragraph 86 of your report, there you say the following about the logistics: "The HVO Main Staff sought from the Department of Defence the realisation of those obligations and tasks set forth by the Decree on the Armed Forces of the HZ-HB. Its demands were primarily oriented around logistics. It sought the replenishment of weapons, ammunition, fuel, food, clothing, lubricants...," et cetera. That's page 86 of your report. And then finally in your testimony on Tuesday, you actually -- you said the following: "There's no doubt that the chief of Main Staff reported to the head of the Department of Defence with regard to the supply of material, that is, supply of weapons, ammunition, fuel ...," et cetera. Sir, can we agree from these quotes that the HVO Defence Department was the primary department for providing the logistics of the HVO armed forces?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you mean the HVO as an executive body? I'm not sure I understood you correctly. Do you mean the HVO as an executive body?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I'm talking about the HVO Defence Department. Was the HVO Defence Department not the primary department for providing logistics to the HVO armed forces?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the department, in the Defence Department within the HVO, yes, it was the main body.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And can we agree that where it concerns the supply of combat equipment, that the Defence Department was, in fact, the only responsible department?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what would follow from this provision. That would be its task.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And would you agree that in actual practice, it actually worked that way?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, if you show me another document -- well, that should have been what it was like, in practice, but I have to admit that the logistics, or logistics generally speaking, through the Defence document, et cetera, I have actually have seen very few documents about that, so it wouldn't be right if I were to say or give a position that I cannot confirm and bear out with documents. This is how it should have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Very well. But -- and would you agree that Mr. Stojic, as the head of the Defence Department, was responsible for the organisation of the logistics?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: In recording the tasks, that would have been one of the tasks of Mr. Stojic. And we were talking about establishment. We know the sectors that existed, and the sector that was in charge of logistics, for example, although the main logistics base was within the Main Staff. But in both cases, I have to say that I have seen very few documents on the subject, compared to other sectors. So as far as the functioning of logistics within the HVO is something I'm not quite clear about. It's very murky, not clear at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Marijan, are you saying that Mr. Stojic was not responsible for logistics?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. What I want to say is --

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, there's really no need. The first answer of the witness was, yes, within the frameworks of the department and sectors under Mr. Stojic. There's no need to attack the witness with something he didn't say. Mr. Bos can read the transcript on line 17 to 19 on page 62. He said quite clearly where he thought logistics belonged.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay. So -- well, you're saying that from your point of view, yes, the minister of defence was responsible, but you haven't seen a lot of documents as far as it concerned logistics; is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, and if I compare it to other sectors, on the basis of what I saw, the percentage of logistics, well, is negligible, it's a negligible percentage, which I admit seems a little strange. As far as other sectors are concerned, I can speak of the practical implementation. Here we have the theoretical part through the provisions. So as far as logistics is concerned, the Logistics Department, there are very few documents on the subject, and even those that existed, general documents from which I cannot draw conclusions, but the HVO did have logistics which did function, more or less. That is not something that I challenge.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, let me read out another part of paragraph 86 in your report. You say that: "The commanders of the HVO brigades and often" -- No. "Commanders of the HVO brigades and other officers often appealed directly to the head of the Department of Defence in the matter of supply and manpower, disregarding subordination, and thus going over the heads of the Command of the zones of operation and HVO Main Staff." Would you agree with me, when you state this, Mr. Marijan, that based on this that there can be doubt that Bruno Stojic was the man to approach when it concerned to matters of military supply and manpower?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's how Mr. Stojic is conceived here, quite obviously, within the system. I don't say that Mr. Stojic wasn't in charge of logistics. There were a great number of requests that went to him, appealing to him. Now, the problem is the quantity, how much. But that the logistics existed within the HVO, nobody can challenge that. Nor do I contest it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, on the importance of logistics, I want to put a quote to you from General Eisenhower. He said the following: "You will not find it difficult to prove that battles, campaigns, and even wars have been won or lost primarily because of logistics." Would you agree with General Eisenhower that logistic plays a crucial role in a war?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I read the general's memoir. It's this American vision of the war. And while we're speaking of Americans, you remember how they entered Bosnia in 1998 with that first armoured division and got stuck in the River Sava. I can tell you, as far as logistics are concerned, that as an HVO soldier, I wasn't hungry, I was well dressed.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let's focus on logistics.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you, your investigators have a better and more comprehensive access to that archive, and obviously some things are missing. I can't believe they had never been written, but obviously --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I have been listening to every word you pronounce, and I have tried to connect your words to other information we have heard from other witnesses and things we have read in the documents, and there's something you just said that makes me react. You said, "I was never hungry." Could you confirm that as an HVO soldier, you did not witness any problems related to food supply thanks to HVO logistics?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, what I can say for sure about my participation in the war, as a reserve soldier in the Petar Kresimir, the 4th Brigade in this period, I did not notice that we had any problems with logistics, but you probably know that we were a municipality that was leaning on Croatia. I had relatives in the HVO Jajce, and they did not have the same experience, so there were great differences between regions and between municipalities. The Operation Zone Central Bosnia had a very different experience from the operation zones that were based in Mostar and Tomislavgrad. But I, as a soldier, did not experience any shortages, except for a certain period where we did not have enough ammunition of a certain calibre. So the logistics did function for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Okay. Mr Marijan, let's move to another topic --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And I'm hearing the French again. Yes, I think it's -- I was hearing the French translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, let's move on to another topic, which is Mr. Boban. We've heard some evidence about the role of Mr. Boban, and I'm going to ask you a few questions about this as well. And let me direct your attention to article of -- paragraph 2 of your report, and this is -- and I'll quote from this paragraph. You say the following: "According to the Decree on the Armed Forces of the HZ-HB from 1992, the rights and duties of the HZ-HB President, Mate Boban, are clearly defined in the section 'Feeding the armed forces.' His duties were as follows: 1. Command and control of the armed forces (Article 29); 2. Appointing brigades, commanders, and high-ranking officers (Article 34); 3. Issuing mobilisation orders for the armed forces (Article 37)." Sir, is it your position that Mr. Boban personally and actively performed these three duties throughout the period 1992-1994?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, these three powers, these three responsibilities of Mr. Boban, that were within his remit, first of all, we can say without any doubt that under paragraph 2, we have a large number -- the largest number of documents we have about this. He signed appointments of commanders of brigades and higher up. There's no question about that. It's the basic staffing policy of the highest military echelons of the HVO, that was under his supervision. As of item 3, the issuing mobilisation orders, I know about one case, and we had I think one or two documents about that. In July, I believe, was one. He gave such orders on at least one -- two occasions in 1992. There were not that many, although I believe I expressed some of my doubts a few days ago about that very term, "mobilisation," and the way it was understood by the HVO. And then item 1, which I left aside on purpose as the most important one, it's the command and control of the armed forces. There is a series of documents or perhaps a dozen documents from Mr. Boban which go to this, but they are very early documents. A command and control of the armed forces again brings us to this problem. I know that this Tribunal, although perhaps not this case, had a big problem defining these two things. The very terms tell us that they are not the same. The word "command" is often used alone. I will limit myself to "command" and say that practically from the summer of 1992, we have no evidence that Mr. Boban commanded the armed forces, which means he had delegated his powers. The army functions here, Mr. Bos, the same way a brigade does. The unit is commanded by the commander and, in his absence, the Chief of Staff, because powers are assigned to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What you're saying is important, but I wonder if we don't have a problem with the interpretation here. In order to avoid that there might be a mistake in the interpretation, what exactly did you mean when you said that there is no proof indicating that Mr. Boban no longer commanded the armed forces or that he no longer commanded? What exactly did you mean there? I don't really understand that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is perhaps an interpretation problem, Your Honour. His function, as Supreme Commander, was never called into question. I think we discussed this the first day, the issue of his signature on a series of combat documents that were expected. It's a fact, and at least I didn't see it, that we have very few documents from Mr. Boban in 1993. I wonder if there are any, in fact. There was a document about the establishment of a military district, but not appointments. So obviously some powers have been transferred from him, which doesn't mean that he did not remain the Supreme Commander. He remains the Supreme Commander and everything should be under his supervision. There's no question about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] A question for the archivist. You said that you looked at HVO documents. Did you examine all of the documents? I don't know exactly what the conditions were. Were they all transferred to Zagreb, where you were working as an archivist or did you only have access to the documents that were limited to the restricted circle of the Presidency of HZ-HB of Mate Boban? I'm not -- and only that. I'm not talking about the documents related to Mr. Prlic or the other heads of departments, but only the close guards, so to speak, of Mr. Boban, where he actually carried out -- where he actually carried out his power. Did you have only those documents or did you have other documents? What would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I did have access to the archive, at least the largest part of the archive; I cannot guarantee that it was all. That's the Croatian State Archive, with more than a thousand binders. I know that I went through most of the documents of the Main Staff, the operational documents at the higher level, at least. I even organised them. And we could not separate a certain part concerning Mr. Boban and say that this is the archive material on Mr. Boban, but the bulk of that material, if not all, refers to the Defence Department and the armed forces, to that part concerning the Defence defence. That's exclusively material of that nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the Chamber had enough time, we would gladly take a look at the archive collection to see how it's classified. It might be very interesting, indeed, and we could probably find some very interesting things. But I'm speaking to you as a professional archivist. In the classification of these various documents, was there a special classification that referred to the Presidency of the HZ-HB? Was there a special shelf or several shelves which contained all of the files dealing with Boban and the inner circle of Boban or is it all mixed up with other documents in various places?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, there was a minor part in the archives of the intelligence community, and I believe I singled out 56 or 57 collections that were a basis for later. There's no collection for Mr. Boban, per se. We have documents of his only through the units with which he had communicated. But as for the existence of something that in archival terms would be called the archival collection of the HZ-HB Presidency, there is no such thing. These documents are scattered through the archives.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The reason I asked these preliminary questions was because I had the following question in mind: Did you see documents, such as the agenda of the personal secretary of Mr. Boban, which might have stated, for example, at a certain day, at a certain time, meeting with Boban, Petkovic, Praljak, Stojic, or whoever, followed by, I don't know, subject, military affairs, something like that? Did you see that kind of document?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, I did not see such documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I have a couple of follow-up questions from what you've been saying in the last five, six minutes. One of the things you said before Judge Antonetti asked you a question was that, and I'm quoting now from page 67 of the transcript, you said: "Practically from the summer of 1992, we have no evidence that Mr. Boban commanded the armed forces, which means he had delegated his powers." If that's the case, who would he have delegated his powers to?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: The powers to command the armed forces were transferred from Mr. Boban to the commander, later called chief of the Main Staff, and that is as envisaged by the decree, and that's the statutory decision of the 15th of September, 1992, that we discussed yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, we're not getting a --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, I'm sorry, there is no such provision in the decree. I will repeat what I believe is relevant for a good understanding of the text we're talking about. The decree does not contain a single provision enabling the Supreme Commander to transfer his powers to command and control to the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But witness, what you're saying is a hypothesis that you're expressing or is it based on objective knowledge? Can we imagine that in any given structure, that the Supreme Commander delegate his essential responsibility, his essential power, which is to be the number-one military commander? Does this exist around the world? Do you have other examples?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have the same example in Croatia. The Supreme Commander, before, now, and always, has been the president of the republic. He holds the position of the Supreme Command, but operative control is in the hands of the chief of the Main Staff, and he has --

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I believe it would be useful, to facilitate your understanding -- perhaps it's inappropriate for me to interrupt, but it's good for your better understanding to see what exactly is written on the Decree on the Armed Forces. There is a very similar provision in the Croatian law, in order to distinguish the transfer of powers to command at the highest level.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is really unusual for me to intervene at this moment, and it's unusual for me to support the Prosecutor. It's a very rare occurrence. But let us allow him to continue with his examination, because it is inappropriate to continue presenting one's own case on the Prosecution time. The witness will tell us what he knows and what he doesn't.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just respond to this insinuation. If a Defence team, in its theory, charges a certain accused more than the Prosecution does, that leads us to Article 30 of the Decree on the Armed Forces. It says that the Supreme Commander --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can Ms. Alaburic stop reading so fast and just repeat slowly what she wanted to say?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, Madam Alaburic, you are not testifying. You can recall that the text exists, indeed, but you can't go any further. I remember that the witness is referring to Croatian positive law, and I don't have the text of the Croatian Constitution before me, but it does define the various levels of competency. And from what I understand, it is the head of the armed forces who, under the control of the president, exercises his power. This is the Croatian system. This is not what we are judging here. We are discussing and judging what happened in Herceg-Bosna. It's perhaps the same system, but it could be a different system. So for the time being, this is not terribly clear. I think we should let Mr. Bos continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would just ask that when Mr. Bos is conducting his cross-examination on this particular issue, to just put -- to just make a reference to the particular article. We do have two different exhibits, P 00289, which was the earlier version, followed by P 00588, and of course it would be very helpful -- Article 30 is the controlling article in both of those instances, and perhaps if he could lead the witness in that fashion. Well, not lead him, but cross-examine him, by pointing him -- and then asking him, you know, to give an opinion as to how he interprets.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Your Honours, in fact, I can. We spoke, Ms. Alaburic and Mr. Karnavas, that I had intend to go to Article 30 and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Just do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, I've been interrupted, so that's why I haven't gone to it yet. And in fact, let's move to Article 30, and it's of P 00588, it's the second version, the amended Decree on the Armed Forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, could you look at P 00588 in the Prosecution bundle. So please -- I don't think you have the Prosecution bundle there.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have the document here as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So it's P 00588, Article 30. Let me just read out what it says. It says: "The Supreme Commander of the armed forces may delegate certain tasks of leading and commanding the armed forces to the head of the Defence Department." So Boban -- Mate Boban could actually delegate some of his command authority to the head of the Defence Department. And isn't it correct, sir, that this is, in fact, the only decree -- this is the only article in the Decree on the Armed Forces which regulates the delegation of command authority, and so therefore that Mr. Boban, in fact, could only delegate this authority to the minister of defence, being Mr. Stojic?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: We can conclude from this that he was able to transfer his powers to head of department Stojic, but if you look at these four paragraphs that are very, very important, this section is called: "Leading and commanding the armed forces." We have Article 31 that says: "The leading and commanding of the armed forces shall be carried out through commanders of the armed forces, in accordance with the authorisations given them." Now, that begs the question --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: But that doesn't say anything about delegation. We're talking about delegation of his authority.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But, Mr. Bos, it would be fair, then, to tell the witness "transferring some -- some powers." That's what Article 30 says, "may delegate certain tasks," not all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: That's correct, that's what the article says.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Sir, would you agree with me that based on Article 30, that the Supreme Commander of the armed forces could only delegate certain tasks to the Ministry -- to the minister of defence or to the head of the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honour, indubitably, he had that possibility, but there's another problem. Did he actually do it? In my opinion, first of all, I didn't see any document on the transfer of powers. That should have been published either in the Official Gazette or somewhere, because it's a public matter. It can be done under the table or it can be done at a general higher level and then brought down the chain of command. So we don't know whether any powers had been transferred and which part of these powers may or may have not been transferred to the area of the Defence Department. So it's a possibility for which we have no proof that it was ever used.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So you're saying, well, we haven't seen any official documents on this, but isn't it true, sir, that just looking at the practice and the number of documents that you have reviewed that Mr. Bruno Stojic indeed had a much more active role in the command structure of the HVO armed forces than Mr. Mate Boban? Could you agree to that, just in the actual practice?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, there's no question that Mr. Stojic, within the framework of leading and commanding, as we see in this article, and we have many documents speaking of his contact with the armed forces, but in view of his powers, he has a very large span of communication with units. But there is a problem, I understood yesterday, and I did draw your attention, Your Honours, to this problem. We have two terms here, "leading" and "commanding." I don't think anyone has ever clarified it. "Commanding" is a term that doesn't cause doubts in anyone's minds, but it's a specific term used only in the army. It's a practice that is governed by laws and decrees which gives somebody the right to command and give others the responsibility to obey commands, but it was always said that it was a commander, a soldier, whereas head of department Stojic is head of department. The Supreme Commander is the only one who has the right to command, and he's defined as Supreme Commander alongside being the president of the Presidency.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. President, this is a good time for the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to have our second break of the morning, because it's now 12.30, so I think it's preferable to have the break at this point, 20 minutes'.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So let's resume the hearing. I think Mr. Stringer wanted to take the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning to you and Your Honours and to everyone else. One very brief request, Mr. President. The Trial Chamber has issued its ruling on the supplemental witness summary for the next witness, directing that the summary be filed, at the latest, by tomorrow, the 23rd of January. We'd request that the Trial Chamber direct that the summary be actually filed by 2.00 p.m. tomorrow afternoon. Tomorrow, being Friday, if it's filed late electronically, it won't be processed by Registry or received by the Prosecution until Monday, which defeats the purpose, and so we'd like to ask that it be filed by 2.00 p.m. And if counsel could send a courtesy copy of it directly to us, that would be much appreciated as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KHAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there's no need for an order. We will endeavour to do it by 2.00, and in any event we will send a courtesy copy to my learned friend.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was sure of it, Mr. Khan, that you would do your utmost. Let's proceed now.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, I would like to move now to the topic of appointments of brigade commanders and high-ranking officers, which was one of the three duties of Mr. Boban. And you've stated that -- and it's correct that we've seen a lot of orders from Mr. Boban assigning high positions in the HVO command, but isn't it correct also that a number of these high-ranking military positions were actually -- actually had to be approved by Bruno Stojic, as the head of the Defence Department, before they were actually being appointed by Mr. Boban?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stojic? Well, I don't think I understood you properly.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Maybe things will become more clear if we look at the exhibits, which is P 02477. It's in the binder, and it's one of the exhibits that was shown to you before, I think, in-chief. It's the 20 May 1993 decision on the internal organisation of the Defence Department. It's P 02477. Mr. Marijan, can I advise you to just to use the Prosecution binder and not any other binder, because otherwise we're getting really confused. The document is actually in the Prosecution binder. It's P 02477. There you go. So do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do recognise the document, Mr. Prosecutor, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let me direct your attention to Roman number III, "Special organisations envisaged for the Main Staff," and forms part of this decision, and then under B, that concerns the appointment of several positions, and let me just read out the first paragraph: "Chief of the Main Staff as a deputy, deputy Chief Of Staff is appointed by the president of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna at the proposal of the chief of the Main Staff and with the approval of the head of the Defence Department." And then if we continue, we see it's similar for the chief of the operative sections, operative centre of military intelligence, again assigned by the president and approved by the head of the Defence Department; likewise, for the assistant chiefs for the home guard, and the assistant chief for organisation, personnel, and legal affairs appointed by the president at the proposal of the Chief of Staff and with the approval of the Defence Department. Now, in-chief you agreed that these were all high-level positions and that's why they had to be appointed by Mr. Boban, but isn't is it true that these positions also needed approval from the head of the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. From this, we can see that he gave his approval to these posts.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: That's the only thing I wanted to raise with regard to the appointments. Let's now move to that third duty of Mr. Boban, which was mobilisation, issuing mobilisation orders for the armed forces. I think you've -- before the break, you said that you had seen a couple of mobilisation orders by Mr. Boban, but not too many, and that they all related to 1992. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I know of two of them dating to 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: But is it correct that you didn't come across any mobilisation order by Boban issued in 1993?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember having come across any.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And, sir, and a couple of these orders you've been reviewing in-chief, isn't it correct that the mobilisations -- all the mobilisation orders issued in 1993 were, in fact, mobilisation orders which were signed by Mr. Bruno Stojic?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: 1990 -- well, I'm just reading it. 1993, there are several, several documents relating to mobilisation. I think they date to June 1993, in fact, and I think they were based on an order by the HVO -- a decision by the HVO dated the 10th of June, 1993, I think the date was. Now, I'm not quite sure whether that might be a mistake, whether it was the 18th of June, 1993 --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, I'll help you, Mr. Marijan, but we'll go through all these documents. Let's move first to Exhibit P 01409, and that's an order dated the 3rd of February, 1993; P 01409. Have you seen this document before, Mr. Marijan?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And isn't it correct that this is an order by Mr. Bruno Stojic to conduct a mobilisation in all municipalities of the territory of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna in accordance with the adopted mobilisation plans?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says, although it's not quite clear. It's not a very clear order.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Why is it not a clear order?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this could be interpreted as an order for general mobilisation, and Mr. Andabak, as chief, I think he was in the armed forces as well, that he was in one of the battalions, Convicts Battalion, but I don't know that he did anything pursuant to this order, so I can't say whether this order was actually carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: But have you seen this order before or is this the first time you're seeing this order?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I saw the order before, because I was looking for something in it. But it was a long time ago, and I saw no link to this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, let's move to the next exhibit, then, and I think you've been referring to that. It's 2D 01485, and this is a mobilisation order of 18 June 1993. So, sir, what we have here is again an order from Mr. Bruno Stojic, based on a decision by the government of the Croatian Community from 18 June 1993, and it relates to the mobilisation of military conscripts in the municipalities Mostar, Siroki Brijeg, Citluk, Grude, Ljubuski, and Posusje. And so he commands, under item number 1: "In all above-mentioned municipalities to preform additional mobilisation of all military conscripts up to 40 years of age and send them to the operative formation deployed in the mentioned municipalities." You've seen this document before, have you?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have, Your Honours, I have seen this order previously, and I think I commented on it over the past few days for this additional mobilisation. Now, I'd just like to draw your attention to a problem here, and I also raised that problem earlier on, that we don't have -- the concept of mobilisation hasn't been strictly defined, as it is in Bosnia and the HVO, so it's not clear to me whether general mobilisation, prescribed by Mr. Boban, was an ongoing process, and this is additional mobilisation, or is this a new mobilisation call-up? So it's difficult for me to say. In former JNA terminology, there was the term "dom mobilizatzi [phoen]," which is a sort of additional mobilisation, when the units were already formed, were replenished. And here from point 3, we see that even the older age group is being called to mobilise and replenish the ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So you're saying this may be an additional mobilisation rather than a general mobilisation; is that your evidence ?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, from the order itself, it would follow that it was additional mobilisation, because general mobilisation, by definition, must relate to the whole of Herceg-Bosna, whereas these are municipalities in Herzegovina and they are municipalities, and I've already said this before, which, from June and July, new brigades were established and set up to make things clear in those municipalities. They were made up of -- well, two or more municipalities had a common -- a joint brigade. So this is linked up to that. When all these municipalities withdraw their recruits or the decision was made whether from -- on pressure from municipalities or whatever, but, anyway, each of these municipalities formed a new brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: But so if you think that this is an additional mobilisation, the document that we just saw before, the one of 3rd February 1993, that was a mobilisation for all municipalities, would you consider that a general mobilisation, compared to this one?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you could understand it that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: All right. Let's look at P 03024. We're now moving from 18 June to 30 June, P 03024. Have you seen this document before, Mr. Marijan?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen this document before. The document can be linked to the previous document, the one you showed me, and it relates to Posusje, and from this you can conclude that the order on mobilisation was progressing slowly and was never put into effect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. Witness, could you be a bit more clearly? Either it never came about or it progressed slowly, but there is an inherent contradiction in your last answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on the basis of this document and the previous document, dated the 18th of June, 1993, it states "Posusje," it mentions Posusje, so on the basis of this, without a doubt, that mobilisation of the 5th HVO Brigade, which was what it was called, that it wasn't being mobilised sufficiently quickly. So this is a warning, among other things, because of the explanation given in the introduction to this text. So it became an urgent matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. So that it did not proceed at all, you cannot say and you do not say. You just say, There must have been problems, and that, I think, is borne out. Does one have to order -- is it then possible to conclude on the contrary, that the mobilisation in the other municipalities mentioned in the previous document worked, well, satisfactorily, for Bruno Stojic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, on the basis of this order, one could conclude that, yes, except if another order were in existence. But as far as I know, this is the one -- the document I know which wants to speed it up and says that it's urgent with respect to those municipalities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, this short document raises three problems: The causes, the consequences and the means used to solve the situation. I think that the causes are that there is an attack against Mostar and Bijelo Polje by Muslim forces on the 3rd of June, 1993, at 3.00 a.m., so there is an attack. These are the causes. The consequences seem to be the mobilisation of all available human resources, equipment, and material. This is paragraph 1 of the order. And the means used to achieve the objective are in number 2, in which it is asked to carry out -- to engage all political factors, police forces, and the media. I'm interested in the police forces. What does it mean, when engaging the political forces [as interpreted]? Does it mean that you have to ask [indiscernible] to join the army and bring them by force to the HVO units? Is this the way you understand this order?

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, there's a mistake in the transcript. I don't know how it was interpreted to the witness, but in line 6, 83rd page, it says "3rd June," whereas you said "30th"; right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I quoted from the document. There is a date on the document. Witness, the police forces were used to arrest those who resisted mobilisation. Why are the police forces present, or does that mean that they also have to engage in combat activities? This is the question I have.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, this is a bit unclearly formulated, but at the end of the day, from the name of the document, because it's an order, it was obviously implied that all forces should be employed. It's a bit illogical for me that the police should be taking someone into custody. I don't know how else to interpret this. And from this text, it's also not quite clear. It associates, in my mind, more with the civilian police, not the military police. It says, "order that all resources be used to carry out the mobilisation."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you clarify the number 02? Does this mean that the Defence Department? In the various departments, does that mean that this number 2 relates to the Defence Department? A moment ago, we saw a number which related to an operational zone, and here we have this number 02. Does this relate to the Defence Department?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, 02 is the number of the Defence Department in the structure of the HVO. That's the number it was assigned. Number 1 should be the head of department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, yes. And the head, indeed, you can see that the stamp bears the number 1, which is the head of department.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's number 1, yes, and it is also indicated that this is the 763rd document in 1993. THE COURT: Please continue, Mr. Bos.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Mr. Marijan, in relation to what Judge Antonetti just asked you, I think Judge Antonetti is right when he says that this mobilisation order relating to Posusje is much more related to the events happening on 30 June 1993 than, as you assume, that this is a follow-up on the 18 June mobilisation of -- which you have seen before. Maybe things will be more clear if we look at P 03038. You can have a look at that in the binder, P 03038.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, this is a very important document, and I presume that you -- that you have seen this document before, Mr. Marijan.

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen it.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: What this is is a joint proclamation from Mr. Prlic and Mr. Stojic, sending a message to the Croatian people who live in Herceg-Bosna, and, well, I won't go through the whole text - people can read it and probably have already read it before - but if we look then starting at the end of the proclamation, it says: "The new Muslim aggression on Mostar causes the changes of life circumstances, behaviour, and activities of the military and civil organisation in these territories. Pursuant to the authorisation and the new situation, the head of the HVO HZ-HB Defence Department, Mr. Bruno Stojic, issues the following order: All conscripts from the territory of Herceg-Bosna, no matter where they are at the moment, have to report to the defence offices in their districts or residence or to their units within the next 24 hours." Sir, is this not again, you know, a very good example of Mr. Bruno Stojic, and Mr. Jadranko Prlic in this case as well, taking the lead into mobilising the Bosnian Croats in a defence?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not clearly emphasised as mobilisation. It's a call, an appeal. It's obviously following on the previous one, and it is a fact that it was signed by Mr. Prlic and Mr. Stojic. It's not clearly defined as mobilisation. I don't know if we could treat it as mobilisation or, rather, a request to everyone to return to their units.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Well, regardless of whether we can call it mobilisation or not, and we'll come back to this document to see whether any follow-up was given in response to this proclamation, but -- we'll leave that for now. I mean, clearly it is a call-up to the Bosnian Croats. Would you agree with me on that one?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a call-up.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I would only like to kindly ask Mr. Bos not to suggest what is not in the document. It is a call, but it says on page 2 "In keeping with the authorisation and the newly-arisen situation, the head of department, Mr. Bruno Stojic, issues the following order: All conscripts from the territory," et cetera, "no matter where they are at the moment." I'm sure that Croats are not mentioned anywhere. If the previous one was a call to Croats, it was because it was the Croats who were attacked. But with regard to mobilisation, there is no reference to Croats.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're really anticipating on the question I wanted to put to the witness. Witness, this document is quite astonishing for one main reason. There are two individuals who sign this document, both Mr. Prlic and Mr. Stojic. Now, Mr. Prlic is the president of the HVO HZ-HB, the head of the department. I don't know why the head of the department would sign as well, but -- I can imagine an answer, but I would like to check it with you. Don't you think this document has two elements, two components; a political component that comes under the authority of Mr. Prlic, which is to develop the awareness of his compatriots regarding the attacks by the Muslim forces, and that political element is expressed through the media? In fact, you can see that this is to be sent to the media, this text. The second component is related clearly to the mobilisation, because under paragraph 1(5), the fact that the conscripts must return to their domicile, that there is curfew, and that certain sales are prohibited between certain hours, et cetera, and that the -- then there's mention of the legal situation of individuals. You're a historian and you have seen many different documents, thousands of documents, thousands of binders in the archives. What do you think? Do you agree that this document can have two purposes, a political purpose but also an administrative purpose, because these measures are being taken because of the circumstances?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if we treat this as mobilisation, we know that Mr. -- the head of the department had the duty to carry out this mobilisation, so he's not doing anything that is outside of his authority, and the signature of Mr. Prlic is here, if we look at the addressees. He is the representative of the executive branch. A body that belongs to the executive branch is sending a communication that falls within his remit. It's not the only document we'll see that bears two signatures, and in most cases such documents were created if the matter fell into the purview of more than one person. I must say I did not deal with the purview of the power of the president of the HZ-HB, but it does fall within the remit of Mr. Stojic. He did have responsibilities regarding mobilisation, he was carrying out mobilisation. And as for these other matters, they are probably -- it's possible that they are probably the responsibility of the president of the HVO.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One last question. Clearly, this document was established within the Department of Defence, because the number 02-1-675, shows that it comes after the 673 that we saw a few moments ago. So this document was produced in the Department of Defence. What is more surprising is that at that time Mr. Stojic was also involved in politics, because it was he, himself, or his team members who drafted the political aspects of the first few paragraphs, 1, 2, et cetera, and then they took it, it would seem, to the office of Mr. Prlic to have him sign and stamp the document, to authenticate it, to prove that indeed he had seen it and approved it. What do you think about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document did result after a very hard day for the HVO. I believe you know what it was about, Your Honours. It was the betrayal of another part of another brigade of the HVO in the area of Northern Mostar, Northern Camp, where Muslim members of the HVO betrayed their comrades and crossed over to the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. It was an extraordinary moment when this document, this order, was created.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you have no explanation about the fact that the document would have been prepared by Mr. Stojic and then counter-signed by Mr. Prlic?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no question that this is a document from the Defence Department. We can see that not only from the number, but also from the heading. But regardless of the preamble, it boils down to a call to prepare for defence. If you call it mobilisation, then it's an order for mobilisation with a very long preamble stating the reasons, and we can link that to the example of Posusje, for instance, where people did not really rush to respond to such events, although the introduction of that document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... the same event.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: We'll come back to this document a little later on, Mr. Marijan, but for now you can leave that document aside. Let me move to another topic which I would like to refer to, and it's -- for you, it's paragraph 131 in your report. It's, in fact, the concluding paragraph. And let me quote some sentences from that concluding paragraph. This is what you say: "Stojic was a member of HVO with executive powers, and he did not adopt any kind of political decisions." And then a few sentences later: "As a member of HVO, on multiple occasions he was involved in the activities of this body, when it was requested from the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna to adopt political decisions or to create bodies to help them in adoption of such decisions." In relation to this quote, Mr. Marijan, what I'm curious about is: How do you define a political decision? What, in your view, is a political decision?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in that specific case, and here it was the session held on the 29th of April, 1993, first of all, it's without any doubt the result of the relationship between Croats and Bosniaks, that is, Muslims. I understand a political decision to be a clearly-defined position towards the BH Army and the Muslims. With a clearly-defined position, one can make a political decision and also a military decision, based on which you can start thinking militarily how to do something and what to do. And in Mr. Stojic's case, it defines his task. That's the problem we mentioned a moment ago, the lack of a clear strategy towards the Muslims, in fact the lack of any strategy at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: In your view, is there a difference between a political decision and an executive government decision?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think it was by accident that Mr. Stojic said this, because that session was attended by the top representatives of political parties, the HDZ and the Presidency of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna. I believe that was their first meeting in 1993, and it was the right forum to elicit from the Presidency of the HZ-HB a clear position that could help define a long-term and elements of long-term conduct.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Is it your position that a political decision could only be made with the involvement of the Presidency of the Croatian Community?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it is my view that the party that had won the elections, and from whose ranks these members of the Presidency were elected, was important in making this political decision. The party's position was important to the political decision. However, the political decision could be taken only by the Presidency of the HZ-HB. However, the opinion of the party must have weighed in a great deal.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: So understanding your last answer, so you're saying that a political decision could be taken only by the Presidency? That was my question, and you seem to be agreeing with that; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the Presidency of the HZ-HB should have taken a political decision. In fact, it was their job, their authority.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Now, sir, in your answer a while ago, you said that, in relation to that, that late April 1993 meeting, that you thought that this was the first time the Presidency was meeting since -- in fact, since their existence; is that correct? Is that what you testified?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I said -- perhaps it's a mistake in the text, but as far as I know, although I might be mistaken, that it was -- I think I said the Presidency of the HZ-HB met rarely, but after the date when they adopted a number of decisions and decrees, I think it was their first meeting in 1993. I may be wrong, but I believe it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: We've heard evidence here from members of the Croatian -- of the Herceg-Bosna government, and in fact the Presidency stopped meeting after 17 October 1992 and then never met until the establishment of the Croatian Republic of Herceg-Bosna on the 28th of August, 1993. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But if I remember that document correctly, in its introduction they are listed, and I believe the Presidency was there. Maybe the Presidency of the HZ-HB did not meet in some legislative sense, did not pass any decrees, but if you have the document here, we can check easily.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: That's exactly what you said, they didn't meet in some legislative sense. And we've heard evidence to that effect, so I think you can take that the president didn't meet in his capacity as the Presidency -- the Presidency member in April 1993. So taking that into consideration, isn't it true that a number of important decisions, in 1992 and 1993, were in fact rendered by the HVO government, without the involvement of the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which decisions you mean. I know the HVO passed decisions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Let's look at a decision which -- which I'm referring to. If you could look at P 01146. Now, sir, this is a document which the Court has seen on numerous occasions, and I presume that you have seen this document before as well. Have you?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I saw it in a previous trial. Yes, it's a document I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: It's a document signed by Mr. Jadranko Prlic, as president of the HVO HZ-HB, on the 15th of January, 1993. And let me just read out the preamble: "In accordance with the agreements so far reached and signed at the international conference on the former Yugoslavia, and the agreement on peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the Geneva Accords, the HVO Croatian Defence Council of the Croatian Community of Herceg-Bosna, at its extraordinary session held on 15 January 1993 in Mostar, adopted the following decision:" And then, Your Honour, I won't go into the content of what actually was decided upon, but isn't it true, sir, that this was a decision rendered by the government of the Croatian Community, of which Bruno Stojic was also a member, and that this was, in fact, a very important political decision?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Undoubtedly, this is an HVO decision, and there's no doubt that Mr. Stojic was there. And this is a political decision.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: And then let's move, then, to Exhibit P 01140, which is related to this decision. It's P 01140. It's a document which must be close to that other document in the binder. It's a document signed by Mr. Bruno Stojic, dated the same date as the other order; 15 January 1993. Now, have you seen this document before, Mr. Marijan?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen it before.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: As you can see in the first paragraph, there's a reference to the decision of the HVO HZ-HB number 1, be it says "001-32/93," which is, in fact, the decision that we just looked at P 01146, and let me just go through the document, and let me just read out, for example, item number 8: "The chief of the Main Staff of the armed forces of the HVO and the chief of the HVO Military Police Administration shall be responsible to me for the implementation of this order, and I order written reports to be delivered to me every eight hours regarding the implementation of this order." Would you agree with me, Mr. Marijan, that Bruno Stojic here, in fact, implements the earlier political decision that we just saw through this -- through this decision?

utterances.speaker: DAVOR MARIJAN [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, this decision is based on the previous decision, the government decision of the same date, but as far as I know this decision was not implemented. I believe the HVO annulled it after a few days. It appears as much more vocal than it really was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bos, I'm going to have to interrupt at this point, because it is now quarter to 2:00, and as you know, there is another case afterwards. Witness, we need you to stay. I know you have a programme scheduled for the weekend. I hope you have a pleasant stay, and we'll have the pleasure to have you back in the courtroom on Monday morning. I would like to inform you that we will resume on Monday at 2.30 in the afternoon. Mr. Bos, you will have another two and a half hours remaining, approximately. That is the schedule.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOS
utterances.text: Did you say "2.30," Your Honours, 45 minutes later -- 15 minutes later than normal?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's two -- about two and a half hours remaining, two and a half hours remaining, but it's more or less two and a half hours remaining for your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 26th day of January, 2009, at 2.15 p.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.46 p.m.,
